prompt: What are the best practices for Domain-Driven Design?
completion:
## Domain‑Driven Design (DDD) – “Best Practices” *(based on the original book by Eric Evans, the “DDD in Practice” series by Vaughn Vernon, and contemporary community consensus)* | Area | Why it matters | Practical ways to implement it | |------|----------------|--------------------------------| | **1. Ubiquitous Language** | Keeps the model coherent across the entire organization. | • Every class, variable, test, and conversation uses the same terminology.
• Domain experts co‑author domain models, not just developers. | | **2. Bounded Contexts** | Delimits where a particular model is valid; prevents “cross‑cutting” of business rules. | • Draw context maps.
• Use **Context‑Mapping Patterns** (Shared Kernel, Customer/Supplier, Anti‑Corruption Layer).
• Treat a bounded context as an autonomous module (often a micro‑service). | | **3. Layered Architecture** | Keeps responsibilities separated and facilitates testability. | • **Domain Layer** – pure business logic, no persistence/transport code.
• **Application Layer** – orchestration, commands, query handlers.
• **Infrastructure Layer** – persistence, external APIs, message brokers.
• **Presentation Layer** – UI or API entry points. | | **4. Aggregate Design** | Controls invariants and provides a transactional boundary. | • Define a **root** (the only reference point for an aggregate).
• Keep aggregates small – no more than a handful of entities/value objects.
• Enforce invariants inside the aggregate, not in services. | | **5. Domain Events** | Decouples state changes from side‑effects; makes history auditable. | • Publish events from aggregates when an invariant has been satisfied.
• Subscribe to events for updating read models, sending notifications, or integration with other bounded contexts.
• Persist events for **Event Sourcing** or audit trails. | | **6. Domain Services & Value Objects** | Keeps entities simple and captures operations that don’t belong to any single entity. | • **Domain Service** – stateless, pure operations over multiple aggregates.
• **Value Object** – immutable, equality by value, encapsulate domain invariants. | | **7. Repositories & Factories** | Provides a clean API for persisting aggregates and encapsulates creation logic. | • Repository API: `add`, `remove`, `find`, `list` – no persistence details.
• Factories encapsulate complex object creation (e.g., `OrderFactory.create(...)`). | | **8. Test‑Driven Development (TDD)** | Forces a clear domain model before implementation and guarantees correctness. | • Write **unit tests** for domain objects first (no dependencies).
• Write **integration tests** for repository and infrastructure layers.
• Use **specification tests** to document invariants. | | **9. Event Storming / Domain Workshops** | Rapid discovery of domain concepts and events, surface hidden complexity early. | • 1‑2 day workshops with domain experts.
• Use sticky notes for events, commands, entities, and aggregates.
• Surface boundary conditions, anti‑corruption layers, and context‑maps. | | **10. Continuous Integration & Deployment (CI/CD)** | Keeps the domain model stable while the application evolves. | • Automate unit‑test execution on every commit.
• Deploy integration tests against a sandbox database.
• Use feature toggles to gradually expose new aggregates or contexts. | | **11. Code Generation & Conventions** | Reduces boilerplate but never at the cost of domain clarity. | • Use templates for repository, factory, and event classes.
• Follow naming conventions that map 1:1 to the ubiquitous language.
• Keep generated code in a dedicated namespace and auto‑generate on CI. | | **12. Avoid Anti‑Patterns** | Keeps the model expressive and maintainable. | • **Anemic Domain Model** – move business logic into services.
• **God Objects / “mega” aggregates** – split into smaller aggregates.
• **Premature optimization** – design for business first, then consider performance. | | **13. Documentation & Communication** | Knowledge sharing keeps everyone on the same page. | • Keep domain models in a living document (e.g., a Confluence space).
• Annotate classes with domain terms (e.g., `/** @domain */`).
• Use visual models (UML, Event Storming diagrams) alongside code. | | **14. Security & Compliance** | Domain models often contain sensitive data. | • Apply domain rules for data masking, encryption, and access control.
• Capture security events via domain events for audit trails. | | **15. Performance & Scalability** | Separate read/write concerns to avoid bottlenecks. | • Adopt **CQRS** for heavy read‑load scenarios.
• Use **Event Sourcing** for immutable, append‑only data and replayability.
• Design read models (projections) that are tailored for specific queries. | --- ### A Typical DDD‑Based Microservice Stack | Layer | Tools / Frameworks | Notes | |-------|--------------------|-------| | **Domain** | Java (Spring) / C# (.NET) / Kotlin / Typescript | Keep plain POJOs / POCOs, no frameworks. | | **Application** | Spring Boot / .NET Core | Handles orchestration, validation, command handling. | | **Infrastructure** | Hibernate / EF Core, PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, Kafka | Implements repositories, event publishers. | | **Presentation** | REST (Spring MVC / ASP.NET WebAPI), GraphQL | Translates HTTP calls into application commands. | | **Testing** | JUnit / xUnit, TestContainers | Separate unit, integration, and contract tests. | | **Deployment** | Docker, Kubernetes, Helm | Each bounded context becomes its own pod/service. | | **Monitoring** | Prometheus, Grafana, ELK | Log domain events, track slow queries. | --- ## A Checklist for DDD Success | ✔️ | Item | Why it matters | |---|------|----------------| | ✅ | **Ubiquitous language** used everywhere? | Reduces miscommunication. | | ✅ | **Bounded context** diagram ready? | Guides team structure. | | ✅ | **Aggregates** identified; invariants documented? | Ensures consistent state. | | ✅ | **Domain events** defined for all state changes? | Enables decoupled side‑effects. | | ✅ | **Value objects** encapsulate invariants? | Prevents invalid states. | | ✅ | **Unit tests** for domain only? | Guarantees domain correctness. | | ✅ | **Integration tests** for repository & infrastructure? | Detects mapping issues early. | | ✅ | **Context map** shared with stakeholders? | Aligns on integration patterns. | | ✅ | **CI pipeline** runs all tests? | Prevents regression. | | ✅ | **Documentation** updated with every change? | Maintains a living knowledge base. | --- ## Common Pitfalls & How to Avoid Them | Pitfall | Fix | |---------|-----| | **Anemic domain model** | Move business logic into domain services or aggregates. | | **Over‑engineering with patterns** | Only use a pattern when the problem truly justifies it. | | **Ignoring domain experts** | Involve them at every step; let them drive the model. | | **Tight coupling between bounded contexts** | Use anti‑corruption layers or shared kernel. | | **Lack of tests** | Test‑driven development from the start. | | **Monolithic codebase** | Keep each bounded context as an independent module. | | **Skipping documentation** | Write and maintain domain models in a shared space. | | **Premature optimization** | Optimize only after the business model is stable. | --- ## Bottom Line Domain‑Driven Design is not a silver bullet; it is a disciplined way of thinking about **complex business problems**. The best practices above are **guidelines**—not hard rules. Use them iteratively: 1. **Discover** the domain with domain experts (event storming, workshops). 2. **Model** the core domain; keep it small and pure. 3. **Implement** with clean layers, aggregates, and domain events. 4. **Test** rigorously at the domain level first. 5. **Iterate**—re‑refactor when the business evolves. When followed thoughtfully, these practices lead to a **robust, maintainable, and business‑aligned software architecture**.
